questions.title: What exactly is hyperspherical energy and why does it matter for finetuning diffusion models?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the OFT paper and they keep mentioning "hyperspherical energy" as a key concept for preserving the pretrained model's generative ability during finetuning. The paper defines it as $\text{HE}(\bm{W}) := \sum_{i \neq j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i - \hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$ where $\hat{\bm{w}}_i = \bm{w}_i / \|\bm{w}_i\|$ is the normalized neuron. But I don't have an intuitive understanding of what this quantity captures. Why is this specific measure of pairwise neuron relationships on a hypersphere important for diffusion models? How does it differ from simply measuring Euclidean distance between weight matrices?

questions.title: Why does the autoencoder toy experiment show that angular information recovers images but magnitude doesn't?
questions.question_body: In the OFT paper, they present a toy experiment (Figure 1) where a convolutional autoencoder is trained on flower images using standard inner products. During testing, they compare three ways of generating feature maps: (a) inner product, (b) magnitude information, and (c) angular information. The paper claims that angular information "can almost perfectly recover the input images" while magnitude "contains no useful information." I'm confused about what exactly is being compared here. What does it mean to generate a feature map using only "magnitude information" or "angular information"? Is the angular version using cosine similarity instead of inner product? And how does this justify that neuron directions store semantic information?

questions.title: How does Cayley parameterization guarantee orthogonality, and why can't it produce reflections?
questions.question_body: The OFT paper uses Cayley parameterization to construct orthogonal matrices: $\bm{R} = (\bm{I} + \bm{Q})(\bm{I} - \bm{Q})^{-1}$ where $\bm{Q}$ is skew-symmetric ($\bm{Q} = -\bm{Q}^\top$). The paper mentions this can only produce orthogonal matrices with determinant 1 (the special orthogonal group), meaning it can produce rotations but not reflections. Can someone explain why this parameterization produces orthogonal matrices, and specifically why it's limited to determinant 1? Also, the paper says this limitation "does not affect the performance in practice" — is there an intuitive reason why reflections wouldn't be needed for finetuning?

questions.title: How does the COFT deviation constraint work with the Neumann series approximation?
questions.question_body: In the COFT section, the paper constrains $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \leq \epsilon$ and says they use the Neumann series to approximate $\bm{R} = (\bm{I} + \bm{Q})(\bm{I} - \bm{Q})^{-1}$ as $\bm{R} \approx \bm{I} + 2\bm{Q} + \mathcal{O}(\bm{Q}^2)$. From this, they claim the constraint $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \leq \epsilon$ becomes $\|\bm{Q} - \bm{0}\| \leq \epsilon'$. I have several confusions: (1) What is the Neumann series and when is it valid? (2) How exactly does $\|\bm{R} - \bm{I}\| \leq \epsilon$ translate to $\|\bm{Q}\| \leq \epsilon'$ — what is the relationship between $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon'$? (3) How is this enforced via projected gradient descent in practice?

questions.title: Why does the paper say OFT performs "low-rank weight update" when R-I is low-rank, and how does this compare to LoRA?
questions.question_body: The OFT paper draws a connection to LoRA by rewriting the forward pass as $\bm{z} = (\bm{W}^0 + (\bm{R} - \bm{I})\bm{W}^0)^\top \bm{x}$ and saying $(\bm{R} - \bm{I})\bm{W}^0$ is "analogous to LoRA's low-rank weight update" when $\bm{R} - \bm{I}$ is low-rank. But I'm confused: the block-diagonal $\bm{R}$ has complexity $\mathcal{O}(d^2/r)$, and $\bm{R} - \bm{I}$ is a $d \times d$ matrix. How can $\bm{R} - \bm{I}$ be low-rank? Is the claim that because $\bm{R}$ is block-diagonal with $r$ blocks, $\bm{R} - \bm{I}$ has rank related to the block structure? Also, LoRA explicitly parameterizes a low-rank update, while OFT parameterizes an orthogonal matrix — so how are they fundamentally different in approach?

questions.title: What is the interpretation of block-diagonal R for convolution layers, and why doesn't LoRA have such an interpretation?
questions.question_body: The paper states that for convolution layers, the block-diagonal structure of $\bm{R}$ has "interesting interpretations" unlike LoRA. Specifically, when the number of blocks equals the number of input channels, each block transforms a unique neuron channel, "similar to learning depth-wise convolution kernels." And when all blocks are shared, OFT transforms neurons with an orthogonal matrix shared across channels. Can someone explain this more concretely? How exactly does a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix correspond to depth-wise convolution? And why can't LoRA have a similar interpretation — is it because LoRA's low-rank additive update doesn't decompose nicely per-channel?

questions.title: Why is preserving hyperspherical energy better than minimizing it for finetuning diffusion models?
questions.question_body: The OFT paper distinguishes itself from prior work (Liu et al., 2021) by saying they preserve hyperspherical energy rather than minimize it. They argue that minimizing HE "could destroy the original semantic structures" because minimum HE means neurons are uniformly spaced on the hypersphere. For classification, uniform spacing is desirable to avoid redundancy. But for finetuning a pretrained diffusion model, the pretrained structure already encodes useful knowledge. I have two questions: (1) Why would uniform spacing destroy semantic information — doesn't it just remove redundancy? (2) How does OFT actually guarantee that HE is preserved, not just approximately? Is it exact or just close to zero?

questions.title: In re-scaled OFT, why is the diagonal matrix D applied on the right of W^0 rather than the left?
questions.question_body: The paper proposes re-scaled OFT with forward pass $\bm{z} = (\bm{R}\bm{W}^0\bm{D})^\top \bm{x}$ where $\bm{D} = \text{diag}(s_1, \dots, s_n)$ is a learnable diagonal matrix. There's an errata note saying the camera-ready version mistakenly wrote $\bm{z} = (\bm{D}\bm{R}\bm{W}^0)^\top \bm{x}$. I want to understand the difference: if $\bm{W}^0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times n}$, then $\bm{D} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ scales the output neurons (columns of $\bm{W}^0$), whereas $\bm{D}$ on the left would require it to be $\mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ and scale input dimensions. Is the correct version scaling each output neuron's magnitude independently? And why is this compatible with preserving hyperspherical energy — because scaling neuron magnitudes doesn't affect normalized neuron angles?

questions.title: How does the 2D Fourier transform analogy justify using angular information for finetuning?
questions.question_body: The paper draws an analogy to 2D Fourier transform, saying that the phase spectrum (angular information) preserves the major part of semantics, and that the phase spectrum along with a random magnitude spectrum can reconstruct an image without losing semantics. I find this analogy confusing in the context of neural network finetuning. The Fourier transform decomposes images into frequency components — what is the neural network analog of "phase" and "magnitude" here? Are neuron directions the analog of phase and neuron magnitudes the analog of magnitude spectrum? If so, this seems like a loose analogy. Can someone clarify whether this is meant as a rigorous connection or just intuition, and how it specifically motivates OFT?

questions.title: Why does OFT converge faster than LoRA or ControlNet — is there a theoretical reason or just empirical observation?
questions.question_body: The paper shows that OFT and COFT converge significantly faster than LoRA, ControlNet, and T2I-Adapter in both subject-driven and controllable generation tasks. They offer two explanations: (1) changing neuron directions is the most effective way to modify semantics, which is what OFT does; and (2) OFT can be viewed as finetuning on a smooth hypersphere manifold, yielding a better optimization landscape. The second point cites Liu et al. (2021). Can someone elaborate on why optimizing on a hypersphere manifold leads to better optimization landscapes? Is this related to the absence of saddle points, the curvature of the manifold, or something else? And is there any formal analysis, or is this purely empirical?

questions.title: What does the paper mean by "no additional inference overhead" and how does merging R into W^0 work?
questions.question_body: The paper claims OFT introduces no additional inference overhead because "we can simply multiply the learned orthogonal matrix $\bm{R}$ into the pretrained weight matrix $\bm{W}^0$ and obtain an equivalent weight matrix $\bm{W} = \bm{R}\bm{W}^0$." This makes sense in principle, but I'm confused about how this works with the block-diagonal structure. If $\bm{R}$ is block-diagonal with $r$ blocks, does merging still produce a regular weight matrix $\bm{W}$? Also, ControlNet introduces additional network branches, which is why it has overhead. LoRA also can be merged — so does LoRA also have no inference overhead? How does OFT's "no overhead" claim differ from LoRA's?

questions.title: Why is the hyperspherical energy defined with inverse distance, and what happens when two neurons are identical?
questions.question_body: The hyperspherical energy is defined as $\text{HE}(\bm{W}) = \sum_{i \neq j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i - \hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$. This uses inverse Euclidean distance between normalized neurons. I have several concerns: (1) What happens when two neurons $\hat{\bm{w}}_i$ and $\hat{\bm{w}}_j$ are identical or nearly identical? The term would blow up to infinity. (2) Why inverse distance rather than, say, cosine similarity directly? (3) Does the paper address numerical stability of this computation? (4) Is this a standard definition from the hyperspherical energy literature, and if so, what's the motivation for this specific form?
